tool.name: PHP
tool.tagline: Pragmatic server-side language that powers a large share of the web
tool.description: PHP is a dynamically typed language built for the web: every request runs a script that reads input and produces a response. Modern PHP has strict types, enums, readonly classes, attributes and a JIT, and an ecosystem built around Composer, Laravel and Symfony. It runs WordPress, Wikipedia and countless business applications, so it is one of the most employable back-end skills.

concepts.name: Running PHP
concepts.summary: Write your first PHP program, run it from the terminal, and see how the <?php tag and echo work.
concepts.why: Every PHP program, from a small script to a big website, is a text file that PHP reads and carries out from top to bottom.
concepts.body:
A **program** is a list of instructions for the computer. It is written in a **programming language**: a precise, limited language that both people and computers can read. PHP is a programming language made for building websites, and it runs a large share of the web, including WordPress.

You write PHP in an ordinary text file whose name ends in `.php`. That human-readable text is called **source code**. A program called the PHP **interpreter** reads the file and carries out its instructions one by one, from top to bottom. A short program run like this is often called a **script**.

You start the interpreter from a **terminal**: a window where you type commands instead of clicking (Terminal on macOS and Linux, Windows Terminal on Windows). Working this way is called using the **command line**. Once PHP is installed:

- `php -v` shows which version you have.
- `php hello.php` runs the file `hello.php`.
- `php -a` opens an interactive mode where you type PHP lines and see the results straight away.

Inside the file, PHP code comes after the opening **tag** `<?php`. Anything outside PHP tags is printed exactly as written; that is how PHP was first used, as small pieces of code mixed into web pages. A file that holds only PHP starts with `<?php` and has no closing `?>` tag, because anything accidentally left after a `?>`, even a blank line, would be printed too.

Each instruction is a **statement** and ends with a semicolon `;`. `echo` prints text: `echo "Hello!";`. Text goes in quotes, and `\n` inside double quotes means "start a new line". Anything after `//` or `#` on a line is a comment: a note for humans that PHP ignores.

`var_dump(...)` shows a value together with its kind (whole number, text and so on). It is the quickest way to see what your program is doing.

On a website, the same kind of script runs each time someone's browser asks for a page, and whatever it echoes is sent back as the page. The web lesson shows how.
concepts.code:
<?php
// hello.php: run it with  php hello.php
echo "Hello, PHP!\n";                       // Hello, PHP!
echo "Version: ", PHP_MAJOR_VERSION, "\n";  // Version: 8
echo 6 * 7, "\n";                           // 42

var_dump(6 * 7);    // int(42): a whole number
var_dump("42");     // string(2) "42": text, two characters long
# A PHP-only file ends without a closing tag.
takeaways: PHP code goes after <?php; a PHP-only file has no closing ?>
Run a script with php file.php; php -a lets you try lines one at a time
Statements end with ;, echo prints, var_dump shows a value and its kind
pitfalls: Leaving a closing ?> followed by a blank line at the end of a file, which prints that blank line before your real output.

quiz.q: Why should a file that contains only PHP leave out the closing ?> tag?
options: Anything after ?>, even a blank line, would be printed as output
It makes the file run faster
quiz.explain: Text outside the PHP tags is printed, so an accidental blank line after ?> ends up in the output.

quiz.q: What does the PHP interpreter do with hello.php?
options: Reads it and carries out the statements from top to bottom
Checks the spelling of the comments
quiz.explain: The interpreter reads the source code and carries out each statement in order.

concepts.name: Variables and types
concepts.summary: Store values in $variables, meet PHP's basic types (whole numbers, decimals, text, true/false, null) and learn why === beats ==.
concepts.why: PHP quietly converts values from one type to another; knowing when it does avoids a whole family of surprising mistakes.
concepts.body:
A **variable** is a name that holds a value so you can use it later, like a labelled jar. In PHP every variable name starts with `$`, and you create one simply by giving it a value: `$count = 3;`. Later you can store a different value: `$count = 4;`.

Every value has a **type** (or data type), the kind of thing it is:

- `int` for whole numbers (**integers**) such as `-3` or `42`.
- `float` for numbers with decimals such as `9.5`. It is a **floating-point number**: stored approximately, so `0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3`.
- `string` for text in quotes, such as `"Ada"`.
- `bool` for `true` or `false` (a **boolean**).
- `null` for "no value at all".

PHP is **dynamically typed**: a variable has no fixed type of its own; it has whatever kind of value you last put in it. `get_debug_type($x)` tells you what that is.

Arithmetic uses `+ - * /`, and `%` gives the remainder. To join text, PHP uses a dot, not `+`: `"Hi " . "Ada"` is `"Hi Ada"`. Joining text is called **concatenation**.

An **operator** is a sign like `+` or `.` that does something with values. PHP converts values to whatever type an operator needs, which is called **type juggling**: `"5" + 3` is the number `8`, because `+` wants numbers, while `"5" . 3` is the text `"53"`.

Juggling matters most when comparing:

- `==` compares after converting: `"1" == "01"` is true.
- `===` compares the value **and** the type: `"1" === 1` is false, because one is text and one is a number. Use `===` unless you have a reason not to.

In a yes/no check, some values count as false: `false`, `0`, `0.0`, `""` (empty text), `"0"`, `null` and an empty list. Everything else counts as true. Programmers call these **falsy** and **truthy** values.

`??` gives a fallback when a value is null or missing: `$name = $input ?? 'guest';`. A **constant** is a name for a value that never changes, written without `$`: `const MAX = 10;`.
concepts.code:
<?php
$count = 3;          // an int
$price = 9.5;        // a float
$name = "Ada";       // a string
$active = true;      // a bool
$nothing = null;     // no value

echo get_debug_type($price), "\n";   // float
echo $count * 2, "\n";               // 6
echo "5" + 3, "\n";                  // 8   (+ turns "5" into a number)
echo "5" . 3, "\n";                  // 53  (. joins text)

var_dump("1" == "01");    // bool(true):  equal after converting
var_dump("1" === 1);      // bool(false): text is not a number

$user = $nothing ?? "guest";
echo $user, "\n";                    // guest
const MAX_ITEMS = 10;
echo MAX_ITEMS * 2, "\n";            // 20
takeaways: Variables start with $ and can hold any type of value
Join text with . ; + always means arithmetic
Use === unless you really want PHP to convert types
?? supplies a fallback for null or missing values
pitfalls: Treating the text "0" as true: in a yes/no check it counts as false.

quiz.q: What does var_dump("10" == "010") print?
quiz.explain: Both strings look like numbers, so == compares them as numbers: 10 equals 10.

quiz.q: Which value counts as true in a yes/no check?
quiz.explain: Only the exact text "0" is falsy; "0.0" is ordinary non-empty text, so it counts as true.

concepts.name: Control flow and match
concepts.summary: Make PHP choose between paths with if, elseif and match, and repeat steps with for, while and foreach.
concepts.why: Real programs react to their input and repeat work; choosing and repeating are the two basic tools for both.
concepts.code:
<?php
$scores = ['ana' => 91, 'ben' => 67, 'cy' => 78];  // names with scores (arrays: next lesson)

foreach ($scores as $name => $score) {   // each name and score in turn
    $grade = match (true) {
        $score >= 90 => 'A',
        $score >= 75 => 'B',
        default => 'C',
    };
    echo "$name: $grade\n";
}
// ana: A
// ben: C
// cy: B

for ($i = 1; $i <= 10; $i++) {
    if ($i % 2) continue;   // odd numbers leave a remainder: skip them
    if ($i > 6) break;      // stop after 6
    echo $i, " ";           // 2 4 6
}
echo "\n";
takeaways: if / elseif / else choose a path; conditions use === and friends
match returns a value, compares strictly and needs a default for unexpected values
for counts, while repeats until its condition turns false, foreach visits every item
pitfalls: Leaving out default in a match whose value can be something unexpected, which stops the program with UnhandledMatchError.

quiz.q: What happens when match ('1') { 1 => 'one' } runs?
quiz.explain: match uses ===, so the text '1' doesn't equal the number 1, and there is no default.

quiz.q: How many times does for ($i = 0; $i < 3; $i++) run its body?
quiz.explain: $i takes the values 0, 1 and 2; when it reaches 3 the condition is false and the loop stops.

concepts.name: Strings
concepts.summary: Write text in single or double quotes, put variables inside text, build multi-line text, and use PHP's string functions.
concepts.why: Web pages are mostly text, so PHP code spends much of its time building, cutting and checking strings.
concepts.body:
A **string** is a piece of text. PHP has two kinds of quotes, and they behave differently.

Single quotes keep text exactly as written: `'Hello $name'` prints a dollar sign and the word name. Double quotes look inside: `"Hello $name"` puts in the value of `$name`. Putting values into text like this is **string interpolation**. For anything more than a plain variable, wrap it in braces: `"Total: {$order['total']}"`.

Double quotes also understand **escape sequences**, short codes that stand for special characters: `\n` starts a new line, `\t` is a tab, `\"` is a quote mark.

For longer text over several lines, use a **heredoc** (short for here document): start with `<<<TXT`, write the lines, and end with `TXT;`. It works like double quotes. If you indent the closing `TXT;`, that much indentation is removed from every line.

Join strings with `.`, and add to the end of one with `.=`: `$s .= "!";`.

PHP comes with many ready-made **functions**: named actions you use by writing the name and putting the input in parentheses. `strtoupper("hi")` gives `"HI"`. Handy ones for text:

- `str_contains`, `str_starts_with` and `str_ends_with` check for a piece of text.
- `strtoupper`, `trim` (removes spaces at both ends), `str_replace` and `substr` (cuts out a part).
- `explode(',', $s)` splits text into a list of pieces; `implode(', ', $pieces)` glues pieces together.
- `sprintf` and `number_format` format numbers: `number_format(1234.5, 2)` gives `"1,234.50"`.

Each position in a string has a number, its **index**, counting from 0: `$s[0]` is the first character and `$s[-1]` the last (strictly, the first and last byte; see below).

One catch: computers store text as **bytes**, small numbers. With **UTF-8**, the usual way to store text, plain letters take one byte, but letters like `é` or `ë` take two. `strlen` counts bytes, so `strlen('Zoë')` is 4. For text in human languages, use the `mb_` versions (`mb_strlen`, `mb_substr`, `mb_strtoupper`), which count real characters.
concepts.code:
<?php
$name = 'Zoë';
$total = 1234.5;

echo 'Hi $name', "\n";            // Hi $name   (single quotes: as written)
echo "Hi $name!\n";               // Hi Zoë!    (double quotes: value put in)
echo "Total: " . number_format($total, 2) . "\n";  // Total: 1,234.50

$text = <<<TXT
    Order for $name:
      - tea
    TXT;
echo $text, "\n";   // the closing marker's indentation is removed from each line

echo strtoupper("tea"), "\n";                      // TEA
echo trim("  hi  "), "|\n";                        // hi|
echo strlen($name), " ", mb_strlen($name), "\n";   // 4 3  (bytes vs characters)
echo $name[0], "\n";                               // Z
var_dump(str_contains('hello', 'ell'));            // bool(true)
echo implode(' + ', explode(',', 'a,b,c')), "\n";  // a + b + c
takeaways: Single quotes are literal; double quotes and heredoc put variable values in
Use {$expr} for anything more than a plain variable inside a string
strlen counts bytes; use the mb_ functions to count characters
pitfalls: Using substr or strlen on text with accented letters and cutting a character in half; use mb_substr and mb_strlen.

quiz.q: What does strlen('café') return in a UTF-8 file?
quiz.explain: The é takes two bytes in UTF-8, so the byte length is 5; mb_strlen would give 4.

quiz.q: With $name = 'Ada', what does echo 'Hi $name'; print?
quiz.explain: Single quotes keep text exactly as written; only double quotes put in variable values.

concepts.name: Arrays
concepts.summary: Keep many values together in PHP arrays, used both as numbered lists and as name-to-value lookups, and loop over them with foreach.
concepts.why: Arrays are PHP's everyday container: form data, database results and settings all arrive as arrays.
concepts.body:
Often you need many values together: all the scores in a game, or a user's name, age and email. PHP keeps them in an **array**.

An array is a collection of items, each stored under a key. In a plain list the keys are position numbers (indexes) counting from 0:

```php
$colors = ['red', 'green'];   // keys 0 and 1
echo $colors[0];              // red
$colors[] = 'blue';           // add to the end: key 2
```

You can also choose the keys yourself, usually as text. That makes an **associative array**: each item is a **key-value pair**, like an entry in a phone book.

```php
$user = ['name' => 'Ada', 'age' => 36];
echo $user['name'];           // Ada
```

PHP uses this one array type for both jobs, and it remembers the order in which items were added. Keys are whole numbers or strings; a key that looks like a whole number, such as `"7"`, is stored as the number 7.

Reading a key that doesn't exist gives a warning and `null`. Check first with `isset($user['email'])`, or give a fallback with `$user['email'] ?? 'none'`. `unset($colors[0])` removes an item; the other items keep their keys.

`foreach` walks through an array: `foreach ($colors as $c)` gives each value, and `foreach ($user as $key => $value)` gives each key with its value.

Useful helpers: `count($a)` gives the number of items; `in_array($x, $a, true)` checks whether a value is there (the `true` asks for a strict `===` comparison); `array_keys` and `array_values` give just the keys or just the values.

You can copy items out into variables in one step: `[$first, $second] = $colors;`. Three dots copy all the items of one array into another: `[...$a, ...$b]`.

Assigning an array to another variable makes an independent copy: change the copy and the original stays the same. (Objects, in a later lesson, behave differently.)
concepts.code:
<?php
$colors = ['red', 'green'];
$colors[] = 'blue';
$user = ['name' => 'Ada', 'age' => 36];

foreach ($colors as $i => $c) echo "$i=$c ";   // 0=red 1=green 2=blue
echo "\n";

echo $user['email'] ?? 'no email', "\n";        // no email
var_dump(isset($user['age']));                 // bool(true)

[$first, , $third] = $colors;                  // skip the second item
echo "$first $third\n";                        // red blue

$copy = $colors;
$copy[0] = 'pink';
echo $colors[0], "\n";                         // red (the copy is separate)

unset($colors[1]);
print_r(array_keys($colors));                  // print_r shows a whole array: [0, 2]
takeaways: One array type works both as a numbered list and as a key => value lookup
Use ?? or isset for keys that may be missing
foreach ($array as $key => $value) visits every item
Assigning an array copies it
pitfalls: Expecting unset() to renumber a list; call array_values() to get keys 0, 1, 2... again.

quiz.q: After $a = ['x' => 1]; $b = $a; $b['x'] = 2; what is $a['x']?
quiz.explain: Assigning an array makes an independent copy, so changing $b leaves $a alone.

quiz.q: What keys does ['5' => 'a', 'b'] have?
quiz.explain: The text '5' is stored as the number 5, and the next automatic key is one more than the largest number key.

concepts.name: Functions and arguments
concepts.summary: Write your own reusable functions with parameters, return values, defaults, named arguments and type declarations.
concepts.why: Functions let you write a piece of logic once, give it a name and use it everywhere, which keeps programs short and readable.
concepts.body:
A **function** is a named, reusable piece of code: you write the steps once and run them whenever you need by **calling** the function. You have already called built-in ones like `strtoupper`; now you write your own.

```php
function greet(string $name, string $greeting = 'Hello'): string {
    return "$greeting, $name!";
}
echo greet('Ada');   // Hello, Ada!
```

- `$name` and `$greeting` are **parameters**: named inputs.
- The values you pass in a call, like `'Ada'`, are **arguments**.
- `return` hands a result back to the caller, the **return value**. A function that returns nothing is marked `: void`.
- `string` before a parameter and `: string` after the parentheses are **type declarations** (often called type hints): they say which type goes in and which comes out. They are optional, but with them PHP stops with a `TypeError` instead of quietly working with the wrong kind of value. `?string` means "a string or null".

Ways to make calls easier:

- A parameter with a **default value** can be left out: `greet('Ada')` uses `'Hello'`. Put such parameters last.
- **Named arguments** pass values by parameter name and can skip defaults: `greet(greeting: 'Hi', name: 'Bo')`.
- `int ...$nums` collects any number of arguments into one array, a **variadic** parameter. In a call, the **spread operator** `...` does the reverse: `sum(...$list)` spreads an array out into separate arguments.

A function gets its own copy of each argument, so changing a parameter doesn't change the caller's variable. A `&` before a parameter (`array &$a`) passes the variable itself (by **reference**); use it rarely, since returning a new value is clearer.

Variables created inside a function are **local variables**: they exist only inside it. A function can't see the variables of the code around it unless you pass them in. A line `static $count = 0;` inside a function keeps that variable's value from one call to the next.
concepts.code:
<?php
function greet(string $name, string $greeting = 'Hello'): string {
    return "$greeting, $name!";
}

function sum(int ...$nums): int {      // $nums is an array of all the arguments
    return array_sum($nums);
}

function counter(): int {
    static $n = 0;                     // keeps its value between calls
    return ++$n;                       // ++ adds 1
}

echo greet('Ada'), "\n";                       // Hello, Ada!
echo greet(greeting: 'Hi', name: 'Bo'), "\n";  // Hi, Bo!
echo sum(1, 2, 3), "\n";                       // 6
$list = [4, 5];
echo sum(...$list), "\n";                      // 9
counter(); counter();
echo counter(), "\n";                          // 3
takeaways: A function takes parameters, runs its body and can return a value
Type declarations make PHP reject the wrong kind of value
Default values and named arguments keep calls short and clear
Variables inside a function are local to it
pitfalls: Expecting a function to see variables from the surrounding script; it only sees what you pass in.

quiz.q: Given function f(int $a, int $b = 2, int $c = 3), which call sets only c to 9?
quiz.explain: Named arguments let you skip the default for $b and set $c directly.

concepts.name: Classes and objects
concepts.summary: Define your own types with classes: properties for data, methods for actions, a constructor for setup, and objects made with new.
concepts.why: Modern PHP code, and every PHP framework, is organized into classes.
concepts.body:
Real programs describe things, such as a counter, a user or a shopping cart, together with what you can do with them. A **class** bundles that data and those actions into a new type of your own.

Think of a class as a blueprint and each thing built from it as an **object**, also called an **instance** of the class. You create one with `new`: `$a = new Counter('clicks');`. Use `->` to reach inside it: `$a->name`, `$a->increment()`.

- **Properties** are variables that belong to each object and hold its data.
- **Methods** are functions that belong to the class and act on the object. Inside a method, `$this` means "the object this method was called on".
- The **constructor** is the method with the reserved name `__construct`; it runs when `new` creates an object, to set it up.

**Constructor promotion** lets the constructor's parameters become properties directly: mark them `public`, `protected` or `private`.

```php
class Point {
    public function __construct(public int $x = 0, public int $y = 0) {}
}
```

**Visibility** keywords decide who may use a member: `public` (any code), `private` (only this class), `protected` (this class and classes built on it). Keep data private or protected and offer public methods, so the class can check every change.

A **static member** belongs to the class itself rather than to one object; you reach it with `::`, as in `Point::create()`. A class constant is created with `const` and read with `self::NAME` inside the class or `Point::NAME` outside.

A class can build on another with `extends`; this is **inheritance**. The new class gets the parent's members and can replace a method with its own version (**override** it), calling the original with `parent::method()`. `final` forbids that.

Objects are shared, not copied. Assigning an object to another variable, or passing it to a function, gives a second name for the **same** object. To get a separate copy, **clone** it: `clone $obj`. Arrays are the opposite: they are copied.
concepts.code:
<?php
class Counter {
    private int $count = 0;
    public const STEP = 1;

    // readonly: set once here, never changed afterwards
    public function __construct(public readonly string $name) {}

    public function increment(): static {   // returns the object itself...
        $this->count += self::STEP;
        return $this;                       // ...so calls can be chained
    }

    public function value(): int { return $this->count; }
}

$a = new Counter('clicks');
$a->increment()->increment();
$b = $a;                 // same object, not a copy
$b->increment();
echo $a->name, ': ', $a->value(), "\n";        // clicks: 3

$c = clone $a;           // a separate copy
$c->increment();
echo $a->value(), ' vs ', $c->value(), "\n";   // 3 vs 4
takeaways: A class is a blueprint; new creates an object from it
Properties hold data, methods act on it, __construct sets it up
Constructor promotion declares and fills properties in one place
Objects are shared between variables; use clone for a copy
pitfalls: Assuming that passing an object to a function protects it from changes; the function works on the same object.

quiz.q: After $b = $a; $b->count = 5; for an object $a, what is $a->count?
quiz.explain: Both variables refer to the same object, so the change is visible through $a.

concepts.name: Handling HTTP requests
concepts.summary: Read what a visitor's browser sends, such as page addresses and form fields, send back a page, and keep visitor input from breaking it.
concepts.why: This is what PHP does every time someone opens a page, and understanding it makes PHP frameworks far less mysterious.
concepts.body:
When you open a web page, your **browser** sends a **request** across the internet to another computer, the **server**.

The server sends back a **response**: usually the page's **HTML**, the text that describes what is on the page. Browser and server talk in **HTTP**, the language of the web.

On the server, a **web server** program receives the request and hands it to PHP, which runs your script once for that request. Whatever the script echoes becomes the page sent back. Each request starts fresh: variables don't survive to the next one.

PHP puts the request's details into **superglobals**, special arrays available everywhere:

- `$_GET`: values from the part of the address after the `?`, the **query string**. Opening `/?page=2` gives `$_GET['page'] === '2'`.
- `$_POST`: the fields of a form the visitor submitted.
- `$_SERVER`: details such as `$_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD']`, which is `'GET'` when a page is simply opened and `'POST'` when a form is sent.
- `$_COOKIE` and `$_FILES` hold cookies and uploaded files.

All of this is text the visitor controls, so never trust it: check (**validate**) each value before using it. `filter_input(INPUT_GET, 'page', FILTER_VALIDATE_INT)` gives a whole number, `false` if the value isn't one, or `null` if it is missing.

To answer, `echo` the page. `http_response_code(404)` sets the **status code**, a number saying how it went (200 ok, 404 not found). `header('Content-Type: application/json')` adds an **HTTP header**, a labelled detail about the response. Headers travel before the page itself, so call `header()` before echoing anything.

Before putting any visitor-supplied text into HTML, pass it through `htmlspecialchars($value)`, which turns `<`, `>`, `&` and quotes into harmless codes. Otherwise a visitor could slip their own code into your page and have it run in other visitors' browsers, an attack called **XSS** (cross-site scripting).

To try it on your own computer, run `php -S localhost:8000` in your project folder and open `http://localhost:8000` in a browser; **localhost** means "this computer". This built-in server is for testing only.
concepts.code:
Ann&page=2 $name = $_GET['name'] ?? 'world'; $page = filter_input(INPUT_GET, 'page', FILTER_VALIDATE_INT) ?: 1; // 1 if missing or bad if (($_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'] ?? 'GET') === 'POST') { // data was sent to us // JSON is a common text format for data sent by programs $data = json_decode(file_get_contents('php://input'), true); header('Content-Type: application/json'); http_response_code(201); echo json_encode(['received' => $data]); exit; // stop here } $safe = htmlspecialchars($name); echo "

Hello, $safe

Page $page

"; // The tags arrive escaped, so the browser shows them as plain text
takeaways: Request data arrives in $_GET, $_POST, $_SERVER and friends, always as text you can't trust
Set the status code and headers before any output
Pass visitor text through htmlspecialchars before putting it into HTML
pitfalls: Echoing $_GET values into HTML without htmlspecialchars, which lets visitors inject code (XSS).
Printing something before calling header(), which fails with 'headers already sent'.

quiz.q: Why must header() calls come before any echo?
options: PHP sends headers after the page
header() only works in the terminal
Once the page starts going out, the headers have already been sent
quiz.explain: HTTP headers come before the page itself, so the first output sends them; later header() calls fail.

concepts.name: Array functions and sorting
concepts.summary: Transform arrays with array_map, array_filter and array_reduce, and sort them with the right sort function.
concepts.why: Idiomatic PHP leans on the built-in array functions instead of hand-written loops for common transformations.
concepts.body:
PHP ships with dozens of array functions. The core trio:

- `array_map($fn, $array)` runs a function on every value and returns the results. With one array it keeps the keys.
- `array_filter($array, $fn)` keeps values for which `$fn` returns true. Without a function it removes falsy values. It **preserves keys**, so wrap it in `array_values()` when you need a clean list.
- `array_reduce($array, $fn, $initial)` combines all the values into one, such as a total.

Note the inconsistent argument order (callback first for `array_map`, second for `array_filter`), a famous PHP quirk. Named arguments help when in doubt.

PHP 8.4 added `array_find`, `array_find_key`, `array_any` and `array_all`, which replace many manual search loops.

Other workhorses: `array_column($rows, 'email', 'id')` extracts a column from rows (optionally keyed), `array_combine`, `array_flip`, `array_unique`, `array_slice`, `array_merge` (renumbers int keys) versus `+` (keeps the left side's keys), and `range(1, 10)`.

Sorting functions sort **in place**: they change the array you pass instead of returning a new one, and return `true`:

- `sort`/`rsort` sort values and reindex.
- `asort`/`arsort` sort by value keeping keys; `ksort`/`krsort` sort by key.
- `usort($a, fn($x, $y) => $x['age'] <=> $y['age'])` sorts with your own comparison function. The spaceship operator `<=>` returns -1, 0 or 1 (less, equal, greater), and arrays compare element by element, so `[$a->last, $a->first] <=> [$b->last, $b->first]` sorts by two fields.

Since PHP 8.0 sorting is stable: items that compare as equal keep their original order.
concepts.code:
<?php
$people = [
    ['id' => 3, 'name' => 'Cy', 'age' => 41],
    ['id' => 1, 'name' => 'Ana', 'age' => 29],
    ['id' => 2, 'name' => 'Ben', 'age' => 35],
];

$names = array_map(fn($p) => $p['name'], $people);
echo implode(',', $names), "\n";             // Cy,Ana,Ben

$over30 = array_filter($people, fn($p) => $p['age'] > 30);
print_r(array_keys($over30));                // [0, 2]: keys kept

$total = array_reduce($people, fn($sum, $p) => $sum + $p['age'], 0);
echo $total, "\n";                           // 105

usort($people, fn($a, $b) => $a['age'] <=> $b['age']);
echo $people[0]['name'], "\n";               // Ana

print_r(array_column($people, 'name', 'id')); // [1 => Ana, 2 => Ben, 3 => Cy]
takeaways: array_map, array_filter and array_reduce cover most loops
array_filter keeps keys; reindex with array_values
Sort functions work in place; usort plus <=> handles custom orders
pitfalls: Writing $sorted = sort($items); sort returns true and modifies $items in place.

quiz.q: What does array_filter([5, 0, 7]) return?
quiz.explain: Without a callback it drops falsy values and preserves the original keys 0 and 2.

quiz.q: Which call sorts an associative array by value but keeps key => value pairs?
quiz.explain: asort sorts by value and keeps keys; sort and usort reindex, ksort sorts by key.

concepts.name: Closures and callables
concepts.summary: Write anonymous functions, arrow functions and first-class callables, and control what they capture.
concepts.why: Functions passed to other functions, called callbacks, are everywhere in PHP: array functions, web routes, event handling.
concepts.body:
An **anonymous function** is a function without a name, stored in a variable or passed straight to another function. PHP calls it a **closure** (it is an object of the class `Closure`):

```php
$double = function (int $x): int { return $x * 2; };
```

It does **not** see outer variables automatically. List them with `use`, which **captures** them, copying each value at the moment the closure is created: `function ($x) use ($rate) { ... }`. Use `use (&$total)` to capture by reference when the closure must modify the outer variable.

**Arrow functions** (PHP 7.4) are short closures with a single expression: `fn($x) => $x * $rate`. They capture any outer variable they use, automatically and by value. They can't modify outer variables and can't contain statements.

A **callable** is anything PHP can call: a closure, a function name string `'strtoupper'`, an `[$object, 'method']` or `[ClassName::class, 'staticMethod']` array, or an object with `__invoke`. The **first-class callable syntax** (PHP 8.1) turns any of these into a proper Closure: `strlen(...)`, `$this->validate(...)`, `Str::slug(...)`. PHP checks it, and code-checking tools understand it, unlike a function name written as a string.

A closure created inside a method of a class (see the classes lesson) automatically gets `$this`, the current object. Declare it `static function` or `static fn` when it doesn't need `$this`; that avoids keeping the object in memory by accident.
concepts.code:
<?php
$rate = 1.2;
$withTax = fn(float $p): float => round($p * $rate, 2);
echo $withTax(10), "\n";           // 12

$total = 0;
$add = function (int $n) use (&$total): void { $total += $n; };
array_map($add, [1, 2, 3]);
echo $total, "\n";                 // 6

$copy = function () use ($rate) { return $rate; };
$rate = 2.0;
echo $copy(), "\n";                // 1.2 (captured when created)

$len = strlen(...);                // first-class callable
print_r(array_map($len, ['a', 'bcd']));   // [1, 3]
echo get_class($len), "\n";        // Closure
takeaways: Closures capture with use (by value) or use (&$x) (by reference)
fn() => captures automatically by value and holds one expression
strlen(...) and $obj->method(...) create real Closure objects
pitfalls: Expecting an arrow function to update an outer variable; it only gets a copy.

quiz.q: $n = 1; $f = function () use ($n) { return $n; }; $n = 5; What does $f() return?
quiz.explain: use copies the value when the closure is created, so later changes are not seen.

concepts.name: Strict types and the type system
concepts.summary: Turn on strict_types and use union, nullable, mixed, never and other type declarations.
concepts.why: Types catch mistakes where a function is called, and they let code-checking tools and editors understand your code.
concepts.body:
By default PHP runs in **coercive mode**: a simple value (an int, float, string or bool, together called **scalars**) of the wrong type is converted if possible, so passing `"5"` to an `int` parameter gives `5`. Put this as the very first statement of a file to switch to **strict mode**:

```php
declare(strict_types=1);
```

Now only an exact scalar type is accepted (the one exception is an int passed to a float). The setting applies to **calls made from that file**, not to the functions defined in it, so every file opts in for itself. Most modern codebases put it in every file.

Types you can declare on parameters, returns and properties:

- Scalars `int`, `float`, `string`, `bool`, plus `array`, `callable`, `iterable` (anything `foreach` can loop over), `object`, and class and interface names.
- **Nullable** `?User` (a User or null) and **union** `int|string` (either one, PHP 8.0); **intersection** `Countable&Iterator` (must be both, 8.1); combinations like `(A&B)|null` (8.2).
- `mixed` (anything), `void` (returns nothing), `never` (always throws or exits), `static` (the called class), and `null`, `false` and `true` as standalone types (8.2).

A mismatch throws a `TypeError`. Typed properties of a class have no value until one is assigned, and reading one before that throws an `Error`.

Implicitly nullable parameters, `function f(User $u = null)`, are **deprecated** (still allowed, but due to be removed) in PHP 8.4; write `?User $u = null`.
concepts.code:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

function area(float $w, float $h): float {
    return $w * $h;
}

function findId(int|string $key): ?int {
    return is_numeric($key) ? (int) $key : null;
}

function fail(string $msg): never {
    throw new RuntimeException($msg);
}

echo area(2, 3.5), "\n";        // 7 (int to float is allowed)
var_dump(findId('x'));          // NULL

try {
    area("2", 3);               // string not accepted in strict mode
} catch (TypeError $e) {
    echo "TypeError\n";         // TypeError
}
takeaways: declare(strict_types=1) affects calls made from that file
Use unions, nullables and never to describe what a function really accepts and returns
Type mismatches throw TypeError instead of silently converting
pitfalls: Expecting strict_types in a library file to protect its functions from callers in non-strict files.

quiz.q: File A has strict_types=1 and defines f(int $x). File B, without strict_types, calls f("5"). What happens?
quiz.explain: Strictness is decided by the calling file, and B is in coercive mode.

concepts.name: Errors and exceptions
concepts.summary: Throw and catch exceptions, understand the Throwable hierarchy and write custom exception classes.
concepts.why: Robust code fails loudly and predictably, and modern PHP reports most problems as exceptions.
concepts.body:
Signal a failure with `throw new InvalidArgumentException('...')`. This creates an **exception**, an object describing the problem, and stops normal execution until some code catches it. Handle it with `try`/`catch`/`finally` (**exception handling**): risky code goes in `try`, the handling code in `catch`. `finally` runs whether or not an exception was thrown, which makes it the place for clean-up such as closing files.

Everything you can throw implements **Throwable**, an interface (a promised set of methods; see the interfaces lesson) with two families:

- `Exception` for application-level problems: `RuntimeException`, `InvalidArgumentException`, `JsonException`, `PDOException` and your own.
- `Error` for problems PHP itself detects: `TypeError`, `ValueError`, `ArgumentCountError`, `DivisionByZeroError`, `UnhandledMatchError`. These usually mean a bug.

Catch the most specific type you can handle. You can catch several at once, `catch (A | B $e)`, and since PHP 8.0 omit the variable when you don't need it: `catch (JsonException)`. Catch `Throwable` only at the outermost level of the program, such as a framework's error handler, where you record the problem in a log and show an error page.

Create domain exceptions by extending a built-in one, and pass the original exception as `previous` so its **stack trace** (the list of function calls that led to the error) isn't lost:

```php
throw new PaymentFailed('Card declined', previous: $e);
```

`throw` is an expression since PHP 8.0: `$user = $repo->find($id) ?? throw new NotFound();`.

Older functions still report problems as warnings and return `false`. Prefer flags that make them throw, like `json_decode($s, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR)`.
concepts.code:
<?php
class InsufficientFunds extends RuntimeException {}

function withdraw(int $balance, int $amount): int {
    if ($amount <= 0) throw new InvalidArgumentException('amount must be positive');
    if ($amount > $balance) throw new InsufficientFunds("short by " . ($amount - $balance));
    return $balance - $amount;
}

foreach ([30, 150, -1] as $amt) {
    try {
        echo withdraw(100, $amt), "\n";        // 70
    } catch (InsufficientFunds $e) {
        echo "Declined: {$e->getMessage()}\n"; // Declined: short by 50
    } catch (InvalidArgumentException | TypeError $e) {
        echo get_class($e), "\n";              // InvalidArgumentException
    } finally {
        echo "-- done\n";
    }
}

try { json_decode('{bad', flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR); }
catch (JsonException) { echo "bad JSON\n"; }   // bad JSON
takeaways: Throwable splits into Exception (your program's problems) and Error (problems PHP detects, usually bugs)
Catch specific types; keep catch (Throwable) for the outermost error handler
Pass previous: $e when wrapping to keep the original cause
pitfalls: Swallowing exceptions with an empty catch block, hiding real failures.

quiz.q: Which is thrown by intdiv(1, 0)?
quiz.explain: Division by zero is an engine error: DivisionByZeroError extends ArithmeticError, which extends Error.

concepts.name: Interfaces, abstract classes and traits
concepts.summary: Define contracts with interfaces, share base behaviour with abstract classes and reuse code with traits.
concepts.why: They let you build parts that can be swapped for one another, which is how frameworks and testable code are designed.
concepts.body:
An **interface** lists methods a class promises to provide, with no implementation. A class can implement many: `class FileCache implements Cache, Countable`. A parameter declared with the interface's type accepts any class that implements it. That lets frameworks hand your classes the objects they need (**dependency injection**) and lets tests pass in fake versions.

An **abstract class** can mix implemented methods with `abstract` ones that subclasses must fill in. A class extends only one parent, so use abstract classes for shared base code and interfaces for abilities a class promises.

A **trait** is a bundle of methods (and properties) copied into a class with `use`. Since a class can extend only one parent, traits are PHP's way to share code between unrelated classes:

```php
trait HasTimestamps {
    public function touch(): void { $this->updatedAt = new DateTimeImmutable(); }
}
```

Traits are handy for small, self-contained behaviour, but heavy trait use hides where methods come from. Prefer composition (an object holding another object) for anything with state or dependencies. Name clashes between traits are resolved with `insteadof` and `as`.

Built-in interfaces worth knowing: `Countable` (makes `count($obj)` work), `IteratorAggregate` (makes `foreach` work), `ArrayAccess`, `JsonSerializable` and `Stringable`.

Use `instanceof` to check a type while the program runs, and mark overriding methods with the `#[\Override]` **attribute** (a tag in `#[...]` that PHP or tools read; PHP 8.3) so PHP reports an error if the parent method disappears.
concepts.code:
<?php
interface Shape {
    public function area(): float;
}

abstract class Named implements Shape {
    abstract protected function label(): string;
    public function describe(): string {
        return sprintf('%s with area %.1f', $this->label(), $this->area());
    }
}

trait Scales {
    public function scaled(float $f): static { $c = clone $this; $c->size *= $f; return $c; }
}
class Square extends Named {
    use Scales;
    public function __construct(public float $size) {}
    public function area(): float { return $this->size ** 2; }
    protected function label(): string { return 'Square'; }
}
$s = new Square(2);
echo $s->describe(), "\n";               // Square with area 4.0
echo $s->scaled(3)->describe(), "\n";    // Square with area 36.0
var_dump($s instanceof Shape);           // bool(true)
takeaways: Interfaces define what a class promises; declare parameters with interface types
Abstract classes share base code; a class has only one parent
Traits copy reusable methods into classes; don't overuse them
pitfalls: Putting stateful, dependency-heavy logic in traits instead of separate collaborating objects.

quiz.q: A class needs to be usable in foreach. Which interface should it implement?
quiz.explain: IteratorAggregate::getIterator() returns the iterator foreach uses.

concepts.name: Enums and readonly objects
concepts.summary: Model fixed sets of values with enums and build unchangeable value objects with readonly properties.
concepts.why: Enums and unchangeable objects rule out whole families of mistakes, such as misspelled status values or objects changed by accident.
concepts.code:
<?php
enum Status: string {
    case Draft = 'draft';
    case Published = 'published';
    public function label(): string {
        return match ($this) {
            Status::Draft => 'Not live yet',
            Status::Published => 'Live',
        };
    }
}

final readonly class Money {
    public function __construct(public int $cents, public string $currency) {}
    public function add(Money $o): static { return new static($this->cents + $o->cents, $this->currency); }
}

$s = Status::from('published');
echo $s->name, ' / ', $s->label(), "\n";   // Published / Live
var_dump(Status::tryFrom('archived'));      // NULL

$total = (new Money(500, 'EUR'))->add(new Money(250, 'EUR'));
echo $total->cents, "\n";                  // 750
try { $total->cents = 1; } catch (Error $e) { echo $e->getMessage(), "\n"; }
// Cannot modify readonly property Money::$cents
takeaways: Backed enums map cases to int or string; use from/tryFrom to read them back
Enums plus match catch misspelled or forgotten cases
readonly classes make short, unchangeable value objects
pitfalls: Using Status::from() on untrusted input without handling ValueError; use tryFrom and validate.

quiz.q: What does Status::tryFrom('archived') return when no case has that value?
quiz.explain: tryFrom returns null for unknown values; from throws ValueError.

concepts.name: Namespaces, Composer and autoloading
concepts.summary: Organise code into namespaces, install packages with Composer and autoload classes with PSR-4.
concepts.why: Composer is how every modern PHP project gets its dependencies and loads its classes.
concepts.body:
A **namespace** groups classes under a family name so names don't clash: `namespace App\Billing;` at the top of a file, then `use App\Billing\Invoice;` (or `use ... as Alias`) where you need it. `Invoice::class` gives the full name, namespace included, as a string.

**Composer** is PHP's **package manager**: it downloads and updates **packages** (libraries, ready-made code other people publish) and the packages those need in turn. `composer init` creates `composer.json`; `composer require monolog/monolog` adds a **dependency** (a package your project needs), downloads it into `vendor/` and records the exact versions in `composer.lock`, the **lock file**. Commit the lock file for applications so every machine installs the same versions; run `composer install` to reproduce them and `composer update` to move to newer versions within the ranges in `composer.json`. `^3.5` means "3.5 or later, below 4.0".

Composer also writes an **autoloader**: code that loads each class's file automatically the first time the class is used. With PSR-4, a naming standard, you map a namespace prefix to a folder:

```json
"autoload": { "psr-4": { "App\\": "src/" } }
```

Now `App\Billing\Invoice` is loaded from `src/Billing/Invoice.php` the first time it is used. Include `vendor/autoload.php` once in the script that starts your app and never write `require` for classes again. Run `composer dump-autoload` after changing the mapping.

Dev-only tools go in `require-dev` (`composer require --dev phpunit/phpunit`). On the live server (in **production**), install with `composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader`. Packages are found on Packagist, the public catalog; command-line tools they include land in `vendor/bin/`.
takeaways: Namespaces prevent name clashes; use imports a class by its full name
composer.lock pins exact versions: commit it for apps
PSR-4 maps a namespace prefix to a folder so classes load automatically
pitfalls: Editing files inside vendor/; they are overwritten on the next install.

quiz.q: With "App\\": "src/" in psr-4, where must class App\Http\Router live?
options: Anywhere, as long as it is required
quiz.explain: The App\ prefix maps to src/, and the rest of the namespace maps to subdirectories with matching case.

concepts.name: Databases with PDO
concepts.summary: Connect to a database with PDO, run prepared statements, fetch rows and use transactions.
concepts.why: Prepared statements are the standard defence against SQL injection, and PHP's database libraries are built on PDO.
concepts.body:
**PDO** is PHP's built-in way to talk to a **database**, a program that stores data in tables and answers questions about it. You ask in **SQL**, the database language, and the same PDO code works with MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite and others through **drivers** (small adapters, one per database):

```php
$pdo = new PDO('mysql:host=localhost;dbname=shop;charset=utf8mb4', $user, $pass);
```

Since PHP 8.0 errors throw `PDOException` by default. Setting `PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE => PDO::FETCH_ASSOC` makes rows plain associative arrays.

Never build SQL by gluing visitor input into it: a visitor could type SQL of their own and change what the query does (**SQL injection**). Use **prepared statements** with placeholders instead; the values travel separately from the SQL, so they can't change its meaning:

```php
$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = :email');
$stmt->execute(['email' => $email]);
$user = $stmt->fetch();        // one row, or false
```

`fetchAll()` returns all rows, `fetchColumn()` one value, and `fetch(PDO::FETCH_CLASS)` or `fetchObject(User::class)` fill objects of your class with the row's values. `lastInsertId()` returns the new id after an insert, and `rowCount()` the rows affected by an update or delete.

Placeholders work only for values, not table or column names; check those against a fixed list of allowed names in your code.

Wrap related writes in a **transaction**, a group of changes that succeed or fail together: `beginTransaction()`, then `commit()` to save them all, or `rollBack()` in a `catch` to undo them all. PHP 8.4 added driver-specific subclasses such as `Pdo\Sqlite` and `Pdo\Pgsql`, created with `PDO::connect()`, which expose driver-only methods.
concepts.code:
<?php
$pdo = new PDO('sqlite::memory:', options: [
    PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE => PDO::FETCH_ASSOC,
]);
$pdo->exec('CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT UNIQUE, credits INT)');

$insert = $pdo->prepare('INSERT INTO users (email, credits) VALUES (?, ?)');
foreach (['a@x.io' => 10, 'b@x.io' => 5] as $email => $credits) {
    $insert->execute([$email, $credits]);
}

$evil = "x' OR '1'='1";
$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = :email');
$stmt->execute(['email' => $evil]);
var_dump($stmt->fetch());                       // bool(false): no injection
try {
    $pdo->beginTransaction();
    $pdo->exec("UPDATE users SET credits = credits - 3 WHERE id = 1");
    $pdo->exec("UPDATE users SET credits = credits + 3 WHERE id = 2");
    $pdo->commit();
} catch (PDOException $e) {
    $pdo->rollBack();
    throw $e;
}
print_r($pdo->query('SELECT credits FROM users')->fetchAll(PDO::FETCH_COLUMN)); // [7, 8]
takeaways: Use prepared statements with placeholders for every value
PDO throws PDOException on errors since PHP 8
Group related writes in beginTransaction/commit with rollBack on failure
pitfalls: Interpolating a variable into the SQL string passed to prepare(), which defeats the point.

quiz.q: Why can't a placeholder be used for a column name in ORDER BY?
options: PDO is too slow for that
Placeholders bind values only, not identifiers or SQL syntax
quiz.explain: The SQL structure is compiled first and placeholders carry data, so identifiers must be whitelisted in code.

concepts.name: Generators and iterators
concepts.summary: Produce values lazily with yield, delegate with yield from, and process huge data a piece at a time.
concepts.why: Generators let you stream big files and query results without loading everything into memory.
concepts.code:
<?php
function numbers(int $max): Generator {
    for ($i = 1; $i <= $max; $i++) {
        echo "[make $i]";
        yield $i;
    }
    return 'done';
}

function evens(iterable $xs): Generator {
    foreach ($xs as $x) if ($x % 2 === 0) yield $x;
}

$gen = numbers(4);
foreach (evens($gen) as $n) echo " got $n\n";
// [make 1][make 2] got 2
// [make 3][make 4] got 4
echo $gen->getReturn(), "\n";           // done

function both(): Generator { yield from [1, 2]; yield from [3]; }
print_r(iterator_to_array(both()));      // [0 => 3, 1 => 2]: keys collided!
print_r(iterator_to_array(both(), preserve_keys: false));  // [1, 2, 3]
takeaways: Calling a generator function runs nothing until you loop over it
Generators handle huge data one piece at a time and combine into pipelines
Use preserve_keys: false with iterator_to_array after yield from
pitfalls: Trying to iterate the same generator twice; it throws once it has run.

quiz.q: What does calling numbers(4) (a generator function) do immediately?
options: Runs the loop and stores four values
Returns a Generator without running the body
quiz.explain: The body starts only when the generator is first advanced, e.g. by foreach or current().

concepts.name: Sessions, passwords and web security
concepts.summary: Keep users logged in with sessions, hash passwords correctly and defend against CSRF, XSS and session fixation.
concepts.why: Login and password mistakes are the costliest bugs in web apps, and PHP gives you the right tools if you use them properly.
concepts.body:
**Sessions** let the server remember a visitor across requests, for example that they are logged in. `session_start()` gives the browser a **cookie** holding a random session id, and loads that visitor's `$_SESSION` array from storage (files by default, or Redis, a fast in-memory database, in larger setups). Call it before any output. Configure the cookie safely: `httponly` (scripts in the page can't read it), `secure` (sent only over **HTTPS**, the encrypted form of HTTP) and `samesite=Lax` or `Strict` (not sent with requests started by other sites), via `session_set_cookie_params()` or php.ini.

After login, call `session_regenerate_id(true)`. Otherwise an attacker who planted a known session id before login (**session fixation**) shares the authenticated session. On logout clear `$_SESSION` and call `session_destroy()`.

**Passwords**: never store them as typed. Store a **hash** instead: a one-way scramble that can be checked but not turned back into the password. Fast hash functions such as md5 or sha1 are unsafe here, because attackers can try billions of guesses. Use `password_hash($pw, PASSWORD_DEFAULT)` (bcrypt, deliberately slow; PHP 8.4 raised its default cost, the amount of work, to 12) and check with `password_verify()`. When the algorithm or cost changes, `password_needs_rehash()` tells you to rehash at the next login. Argon2id is available with `PASSWORD_ARGON2ID`.

**CSRF** (cross-site request forgery): a malicious site can make the visitor's browser submit a form to yours, and the browser sends the visitor's cookies along. Put a random token, `bin2hex(random_bytes(32))`, in the session and in every form, then compare with `hash_equals()`, which takes the same time however many characters match, so attackers can't learn the token by measuring response times.

The rest of the checklist: prepared statements against SQL injection, `htmlspecialchars` on output against XSS, `random_bytes` and `random_int` for anything secret (never `rand`, which is predictable), and never `unserialize()` untrusted data, since it can create objects of the attacker's choosing.
concepts.code:
<?php
session_set_cookie_params(['httponly' => true, 'secure' => true, 'samesite' => 'Lax']);
session_start();

$hash = password_hash('correct horse', PASSWORD_DEFAULT);
echo substr($hash, 0, 7), "\n";                  // $2y$12$ (bcrypt, cost 12 in 8.4)
var_dump(password_verify('correct horse', $hash)); // bool(true)
var_dump(password_verify('wrong', $hash));         // bool(false)

function login(int $userId): void {
    session_regenerate_id(true);       // defeat session fixation
    $_SESSION['user_id'] = $userId;
}

$_SESSION['csrf'] ??= bin2hex(random_bytes(32));
// In the form: <input type="hidden" name="csrf" value="...">
function checkCsrf(string $sent): bool {
    return hash_equals($_SESSION['csrf'], $sent);
}
var_dump(checkCsrf('guess'));          // bool(false)
takeaways: Regenerate the session id on login and set httponly, secure and samesite cookies
password_hash and password_verify are the only password API you need
Protect state-changing forms with a CSRF token compared via hash_equals
pitfalls: Comparing tokens or hashes with ==, which leaks timing information and is subject to type juggling.

quiz.q: Why call session_regenerate_id(true) right after a successful login?
options: So a session id known before login can't be used to hijack the logged-in session
Because the old id expires at login
quiz.explain: It prevents session fixation by issuing a fresh id once the session gains privileges.

concepts.name: Testing with PHPUnit
concepts.summary: Write unit tests with PHPUnit: test classes, assertions, data providers and expected exceptions.
concepts.why: Tests let you restructure code and upgrade PHP with confidence, and every serious PHP project has them.
concepts.body:
A **unit test** is code that calls a small piece of your code and checks the result automatically. **PHPUnit** is the standard PHP testing framework (Pest, built on top of it, offers a terser function-based syntax). Install it per project with `composer require --dev phpunit/phpunit` and run `vendor/bin/phpunit`.

A test case is a class extending `PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase`. Each public method whose name starts with `test`, or which has the `#[Test]` attribute, is a test. **Attributes** are tags in `#[...]` that tools read; modern PHPUnit (11 and 12) uses them instead of the older special comments (docblock annotations).

- Each `assert...` call is an **assertion**, a check that fails the test if it isn't true. `assertSame($expected, $actual)` compares with `===`. Prefer it to `assertEquals`, which compares loosely.
- `assertTrue`, `assertCount`, `assertContains`, `assertInstanceOf`, `assertStringContainsString` cover most checks.
- `$this->expectException(InvalidArgumentException::class)` before the call asserts that it throws.
- `setUp()` runs before every test to build fresh objects for it (**fixtures**).

A **data provider** runs one test with many inputs: a `public static` method returns named sets of inputs, and `#[DataProvider('cases')]` links it.

Replace slow or outside parts (web requests, sending email) with **test doubles**, fake stand-ins: `$this->createStub(Clock::class)` returns fixed answers, and `createMock()` also checks that it was called as expected. Doubles work best when your classes receive interfaces through their constructor.

Configure test suites and coverage (which lines the tests ran) in `phpunit.xml`; coverage needs the Xdebug or PCOV extension.
concepts.code:
<?php
// tests/PriceTest.php, run with vendor/bin/phpunit tests
use PHPUnit\Framework\Attributes\DataProvider;
use PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase;
final class PriceTest extends TestCase
{
    public static function discounts(): array
    {
        return [
            'no discount' => [100, 0, 100],
            'ten percent' => [100, 10, 90],
            'rounds down' => [99, 50, 49],
        ];
    }
    #[DataProvider('discounts')]
    public function testApplyDiscount(int $price, int $pct, int $expected): void
    {
        $this->assertSame($expected, intdiv($price * (100 - $pct), 100));
    }
    public function testRejectsBadInput(): void
    {
        $this->expectException(ValueError::class);
        str_repeat('x', -1);   // ValueError: times must be >= 0
    }
}
takeaways: Tests extend TestCase; use assertSame for strict checks
Attributes such as #[DataProvider] replace the old special comments
Pass interfaces into classes so tests can swap in stubs and mocks
pitfalls: Using assertEquals where types matter: assertEquals(1, '1') passes.

quiz.q: In PHPUnit 11+, what must a data provider method be?
quiz.explain: Data providers must be public static methods, linked with the #[DataProvider] attribute.

concepts.name: Property hooks and asymmetric visibility
concepts.summary: Use PHP 8.4 property hooks for computed and validated properties, and private(set) for read-only-from-outside state.
concepts.why: They remove most hand-written getter and setter methods while the class keeps control of its data.
concepts.body:
**Property hooks** (PHP 8.4) attach `get` and `set` logic directly to a property, so callers use plain property syntax while the class keeps control:

```php
public string $email {
    set(string $value) { $this->email = strtolower(trim($value)); }
}
```

- A `set` hook runs on every write, including in the constructor. Inside it, `$this->email` refers to the stored value (the backing value).
- A `get` hook computes the value on read. A property whose hooks never touch the backing value is **virtual**: it takes no memory, like `public string $fullName { get => "$this->first $this->last"; }`.
- The short form `set => strtolower($value);` assigns the expression to the backing value.
- Interfaces and abstract classes can declare properties with hooks, e.g. `public string $name { get; }`, so a contract can require a readable property.

**Asymmetric visibility** lets reading and writing have different visibility: `public private(set) int $balance = 0;` is readable everywhere but writable only inside the class. `protected(set)` allows subclasses to write. Unlike `readonly`, the class can change the value as often as it likes.

Rules of thumb: use `readonly` for true value objects, `private(set)` for objects whose data changes through their own methods, and hooks for tidying values (such as lower-casing an email) or calculating them. Hooks cannot be combined with `readonly`.
concepts.code:
<?php // PHP 8.4
final class Account
{
    public private(set) int $balance = 0;

    public string $owner {
        set(string $value) {
            if ($value === '') throw new ValueError('owner required');
            $this->owner = ucwords(strtolower($value));
        }
    }

    public string $label {
        get => "{$this->owner} ({$this->balance})";   // virtual property
    }

    public function __construct(string $owner) { $this->owner = $owner; }

    public function deposit(int $amount): void { $this->balance += $amount; }
}

$a = new Account('ADA lovelace');
$a->deposit(50);
echo $a->label, "\n";          // Ada Lovelace (50)
try { $a->balance = 1000; } catch (Error $e) { echo "read-only from outside\n"; }
takeaways: set hooks normalise or validate on every write; get hooks compute on read
A property whose hooks never use the backing value is virtual
public private(set) = readable everywhere, writable only inside the class
pitfalls: Reaching for hooks on a readonly property; the two can't be combined.

quiz.q: What is true of public private(set) int $balance?
options: Outside code can assign it but not read it
It can be assigned only once
Outside code can read it but not assign it
quiz.explain: Asymmetric visibility makes reads public and writes private, without the write-once rule of readonly.

concepts.name: Attributes and static analysis
concepts.summary: Read and define attributes, and catch bugs before the code runs with PHPStan, its strictness levels and generics.
concepts.why: Static analysis finds type mistakes PHP would only hit while running, which is essential in large codebases.
concepts.body:
**Attributes** (PHP 8.0) attach structured **metadata**, extra information about the code, to classes, methods, properties, parameters and constants: `#[Route('/users', methods: ['GET'])]`. An attribute is a class marked `#[Attribute]`; nothing happens until code reads it through **reflection** (code inspecting classes while the program runs) with `getAttributes()` and calls `newInstance()`. Frameworks use them for routing (which address runs which method) and dependency injection.

The engine itself understands a few: `#[\Override]` (8.3), `#[\SensitiveParameter]` (8.2, hides a value in stack traces), `#[\Deprecated]` (8.4, emits deprecation notices for your own functions) and `#[\AllowDynamicProperties]`.

**PHPStan** (and Psalm) do **static analysis**: they check code by reading it, without running it. Install with `composer require --dev phpstan/phpstan` and run `vendor/bin/phpstan analyse src --level 6`. Levels go from 0 (basic checks) to 10 (strictest, also treating `mixed` strictly); raise the level gradually, and use a baseline file (a list of existing problems to ignore for now) to adopt it in older code.

PHP's native types can't express everything, so analysers read **PHPDoc types**:

- `@param list<User> $users`, `@return array<string, int>`, `non-empty-string`, `positive-int`.
- Array shapes: `array{id: int, name: string}`.
- **Generics**: `@template T` on a class or function declares a placeholder type `T`, then `@param class-string<T> $class` and `@return T`.

These annotations are ignored at runtime but make the analyser, and your editor, understand collections and factories precisely.
concepts.code:
<?php
#[Attribute(Attribute::TARGET_METHOD)]
final class Route {
    public function __construct(public string $path, public array $methods = ['GET']) {}
}

final class UserController {
    #[Route('/users', methods: ['GET', 'HEAD'])]
    public function index(): string { return 'list'; }
}

foreach ((new ReflectionClass(UserController::class))->getMethods() as $m) {
    foreach ($m->getAttributes(Route::class) as $attr) {
        $route = $attr->newInstance();
        echo implode('|', $route->methods), " {$route->path} -> {$m->name}\n";
    }
}
// GET|HEAD /users -> index
/**
 * @template T of object
 * @param class-string<T> $class
 * @return T
 */
function make(string $class): object { return new $class(); }
$c = make(UserController::class);   // PHPStan knows $c is UserController
takeaways: Attributes are metadata classes read via Reflection
PHPStan levels 0-10 let you tighten checks gradually
@template and class-string<T> express generics PHP can't
pitfalls: Expecting an attribute to do something by itself; it only matters when code reads it.

quiz.q: When is the constructor of an attribute class like Route executed?
options: When the annotated method is called
quiz.explain: Attributes are lazy metadata; they are instantiated only when read through Reflection.

concepts.name: Request lifecycle, SAPIs and PHP-FPM
concepts.summary: Understand how a request reaches PHP through a SAPI, PHP-FPM's process model and long-running worker modes.
concepts.why: Capacity planning, timeouts and many production incidents come down to how PHP processes are run.
concepts.body:
PHP talks to the outside world through a **SAPI** (Server API), the layer that connects it to whatever starts it: `cli` for scripts, `fpm-fcgi` for PHP-FPM, `apache2handler` for mod_php, and embedded SAPIs like FrankenPHP's. `PHP_SAPI` tells you which one you are in.

The classic model is **shared-nothing**: for every request PHP initialises the request state, compiles the script (or takes it ready-made from OPcache, the next lesson), runs it, sends the output and then frees all request memory. Nothing leaks between requests, so one request can't damage the next user's data, and a crash affects one request.

**PHP-FPM** runs a main (master) **process** and a pool of **worker** processes; each worker handles one request at a time. The web server (nginx, Caddy) forwards requests to it over FastCGI, a protocol made for this. Key pool settings:

- `pm = dynamic | static | ondemand` and `pm.max_children`: the most requests handled at the same time. Size it as available RAM divided by memory per worker.
- `pm.max_requests` restarts each worker after that many requests, to contain slow **memory leaks**.
- `request_terminate_timeout` and `max_execution_time` cap runaway scripts, and `memory_limit` caps memory per request.

Because a worker blocks while waiting on a database or API, slow I/O directly reduces throughput. The status page (`pm.status_path`) and slow log (`request_slowlog_timeout`) show where time goes.

**Worker modes** (FrankenPHP workers, RoadRunner, Swoole, Laravel Octane) boot the app once and keep it in memory across requests. They are much faster, but give up shared-nothing: static properties, **singletons** (objects created once and shared) and globals now persist, and must be reset per request.
concepts.code:
; /etc/php/8.4/fpm/pool.d/www.conf (excerpt)
[www]
listen = /run/php/php8.4-fpm.sock
pm = dynamic
; ~ (RAM for PHP) / (avg worker RSS), e.g. 4 GB / 80 MB = 50
pm.max_children = 50
pm.start_servers = 10
pm.min_spare_servers = 5
pm.max_spare_servers = 15
; recycle workers to contain leaks
pm.max_requests = 1000
request_terminate_timeout = 30s
request_slowlog_timeout = 5s
slowlog = /var/log/php-fpm/slow.log
pm.status_path = /fpm-status
php_admin_value[memory_limit] = 256M
takeaways: PHP runs behind a SAPI; FPM uses a pool of single-request worker processes
pm.max_children bounds concurrency; size it from memory per worker
Worker modes boot once and trade shared-nothing safety for speed
pitfalls: Raising pm.max_children beyond available RAM, causing swapping or OOM kills under load.

quiz.q: With pm.max_children = 20 and every request waiting 1 s on a slow API, roughly how many requests per second can the pool serve?
quiz.explain: Each worker handles one request at a time, so 20 workers blocked for 1 s each give about 20 req/s.

quiz.q: What changes when an app runs in a worker mode like FrankenPHP or Octane?
options: Each request gets a new process
Static and singleton state persists across requests
quiz.explain: The app stays in memory, so anything stored in statics or singletons leaks into later requests unless reset.

concepts.name: Values, references and memory
concepts.summary: See how PHP stores values: copy-on-write, reference counting, PHP references, and the cycle collector.
concepts.why: Knowing the memory model explains performance surprises, memory leaks in workers and odd reference bugs.
concepts.body:
Internally every PHP value is a **zval**: a small C struct (a fixed group of fields) holding a type tag and either the value itself (int, float, bool, null) or a **pointer**, the memory address of a bigger structure (string, array, object) that keeps a **reference count**: the number of variables using it.

Arrays and strings use **copy-on-write**. `$b = $a` just adds 1 to the reference count; the actual copy happens only when one side is modified. That's why passing large arrays to functions is cheap as long as the function only reads them. Packed arrays (keys 0, 1, 2... in order) use less memory than **hash tables**, which arrays with other keys use.

**Objects** are different: the zval holds a handle to the object, so copies of the variable share one object. This is not the same as a reference.

A PHP **reference** (`&`) makes two names point to the same zval slot. References disable copy-on-write for that value and have surprising effects. The classic one: after `foreach ($arr as &$v)`, `$v` still references the last element, and a later `foreach ($arr as $v)` overwrites it. Always `unset($v)` after a by-reference loop, or avoid references entirely.

Memory is freed as soon as a refcount drops to zero. **Cycles** (an object that references itself, parent and child pointing to each other) never reach zero, so PHP runs a cycle collector when its root buffer, a list of suspects, fills (10,000 entries). `gc_collect_cycles()` forces a run and `gc_status()` reports statistics. In short requests leaks rarely matter; in long-running workers and queue consumers they accumulate, so measure with `memory_get_usage()` and break cycles explicitly or use `WeakMap` (a map that doesn't keep its keys alive).
concepts.code:
<?php
$a = range(1, 100_000);
$before = memory_get_usage();
$b = $a;                                   // no copy yet (refcount 2)
echo memory_get_usage() - $before, "\n";   // 0
$b[] = 1;                                  // now the array is separated
echo memory_get_usage() - $before > 1_000_000 ? "copied\n" : "shared\n"; // copied

$list = [1, 2, 3];
foreach ($list as &$v) { $v *= 10; }
foreach ($list as $v) {}                   // reuses the reference!
print_r($list);                            // [10, 20, 20]

class Node { public ?Node $other = null; }
$x = new Node(); $y = new Node();
$x->other = $y; $y->other = $x;            // cycle
unset($x, $y);
echo gc_collect_cycles(), "\n";            // 2 objects freed
takeaways: Arrays and strings are copy-on-write: copies are free until modified
Objects are shared handles; & references are a different, rarer mechanism
Reference cycles need the cycle collector; long-running workers must watch memory
pitfalls: Leaving a by-reference foreach variable alive, then reusing its name in another loop.

quiz.q: After $b = $a for a large array, when does PHP actually copy the data?
quiz.explain: Copy-on-write shares the array until a write forces separation.

quiz.q: Why is foreach ($arr as &$v) followed by foreach ($arr as $v) dangerous?
options: The second loop is a syntax error
$v still references the last element, so the second loop overwrites it
It converts the array to an object
quiz.explain: The second loop assigns each element to $v, which is still a reference to the last slot.

concepts.name: OPcache, preloading and the JIT
concepts.summary: Configure OPcache for production, use preloading, and know when the JIT helps and when it doesn't.
concepts.why: OPcache is the single biggest PHP performance setting, and misconfiguring it causes stale-code deployments.
concepts.body:
PHP compiles each file to **opcodes**, simple internal instructions, before running it. **OPcache** keeps the compiled opcodes in memory shared by all worker processes, so later requests skip reading and compiling the files again. It should always be on in production (`opcache.enable=1`); it's typically a several-fold speedup.

Important settings:

- `opcache.memory_consumption` and `opcache.max_accelerated_files` must fit your whole codebase including `vendor/`. Check `opcache_get_status()` for a full cache or a poor hit rate (the share of lookups served from the cache).
- `opcache.validate_timestamps=0` stops PHP from checking file modification times, which saves a file-system check per file, but then new code is not seen until you reload PHP-FPM or call `opcache_reset()`. Make that part of every deploy.
- `opcache.interned_strings_buffer` holds one shared copy of repeated strings such as class and method names.

**Preloading** (`opcache.preload`, PHP 7.4) runs a script at server start that loads chosen classes into memory permanently, so they are prepared once instead of on every request. Gains are modest for most apps, and any change requires a full restart.

The **JIT** compiler (PHP 8.0) turns frequently run opcodes into machine code, the processor's own instructions. Enable it with `opcache.jit=tracing` and a non-zero `opcache.jit_buffer_size`. It speeds up **CPU-bound** work, limited by calculation rather than waiting, such as math, image processing or parsers dramatically, but typical web requests spend their time waiting on databases and the network, so the gain there is small. Always benchmark your workload before and after.

`opcache.enable_cli` is off by default, as one-off CLI scripts rarely benefit.
concepts.code:
; php.ini production excerpt
opcache.enable=1
opcache.memory_consumption=256
opcache.interned_strings_buffer=32
opcache.max_accelerated_files=50000
; deploys must then reload FPM or call opcache_reset()
opcache.validate_timestamps=0
opcache.preload=/var/www/app/preload.php
opcache.preload_user=www-data
; JIT: helps CPU-bound code
opcache.jit=tracing
opcache.jit_buffer_size=64M

; check from PHP:
;   $s = opcache_get_status(false);
;   $s['opcache_statistics']['opcache_hit_rate'];   e.g. 99.9
;   $s['memory_usage']['free_memory'];
takeaways: OPcache caches compiled opcodes in shared memory and must be on in production
With validate_timestamps=0, every deploy needs an FPM reload or opcache_reset
The JIT pays off for CPU-bound code, much less for I/O-bound web requests
pitfalls: Setting validate_timestamps=0 and deploying without reloading PHP, so old code keeps running.

quiz.q: A deploy copies new files but users still see old behaviour. OPcache has validate_timestamps=0. What fixes it?
quiz.explain: Without timestamp checks OPcache keeps serving cached opcodes until it is reset.

concepts.name: Fibers and async PHP
concepts.summary: Understand Fibers, PHP's primitive for pausable functions, and how async libraries build event loops on them.
concepts.why: Async libraries like AMPHP and ReactPHP use Fibers to run many network operations at once while the code still reads like ordinary step-by-step code.
concepts.code:
<?php
// A tiny round-robin scheduler: two "tasks" interleave cooperatively
function task(string $name, int $steps): Fiber {
    return new Fiber(function () use ($name, $steps): string {
        for ($i = 1; $i <= $steps; $i++) {
            echo "$name step $i\n";
            Fiber::suspend();          // yield control back to the loop
        }
        return "$name finished";
    });
}

$queue = [task('A', 2), task('B', 3)];
foreach ($queue as $f) $f->start();   // A step 1, B step 1

while ($queue) {
    $f = array_shift($queue);
    $f->resume();
    if ($f->isTerminated()) echo $f->getReturn(), "\n";
    else $queue[] = $f;
}
// A step 2, B step 2, A finished, B step 3, B finished
takeaways: A Fiber can suspend from anywhere in its call stack and be resumed later
Fibers are cooperative and single-threaded: concurrency, not parallelism
Event loops like Revolt use Fibers to make async I/O look synchronous
pitfalls: Calling blocking functions (sleep, PDO) inside an async app, which stalls every fiber.

quiz.q: What does $fiber->start() return?
options: The value passed to the first Fiber::suspend(), or null if the fiber finishes
quiz.explain: start() runs until the first suspend and returns the value given to it; the return value is read with getReturn().
